results.name: power_of_two_specificity
results.description: Among sets whose examples are all powers of 2 (2..64), yes rate to non-example powers of 2 minus yes rate to other even non-example targets; observed above the null means people commit to the specific "powers of 2" rule more sharply than the model (which leaks to "even"/ranges), below means the model over-commits to the specific rule.
results.code:
# name: power_of_two_specificity
# description: Among sets whose examples are all powers of 2 (2..64), yes rate to non-example powers of 2 minus yes rate to other even non-example targets; observed above the null means people commit to the specific "powers of 2" rule more sharply than the model (which leaks to "even"/ranges), below means the model over-commits to the specific rule.
def test_statistic(df):
    p2 = {"2", "4", "8", "16", "32", "64"}
    ex = df["number_set"].str.split(",")
    all_p2 = np.array([set(e) <= p2 for e in ex])
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    tgt = t.astype(str)
    is_ex = np.array([s in e for s, e in zip(tgt, ex)])
    is_p2 = np.isin(t, [2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64])
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    a = all_p2 & ~is_ex & is_p2
    b = all_p2 & ~is_ex & ~is_p2 & (t % 2 == 0)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: switch_trial_carryover
results.description: Among consecutive within-participant trial pairs where the example set CHANGES, yes rate after a yes minus yes rate after a no; observed above the null means response-level perseveration that carries across different sets (not explained by repeated-set stimulus similarity), which the trial-independent model under-produces.
results.code:
# name: switch_trial_carryover
# description: Among consecutive within-participant trial pairs where the example set CHANGES, yes rate after a yes minus yes rate after a no; observed above the null means response-level perseveration that carries across different sets (not explained by repeated-set stimulus similarity), which the trial-independent model under-produces.
def test_statistic(df):
    ti = df["trial_index"].to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    s = df["number_set"].to_numpy()
    ok = (ti[1:] > ti[:-1]) & (s[1:] != s[:-1])
    prev, cur = r[:-1][ok], r[1:][ok]
    if (prev == 1).sum() == 0 or (prev == 0).sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(cur[prev == 1].mean() - cur[prev == 0].mean())

results.name: repeat_exposure_decline
results.description: Within each participant x set (participants start where trial_index resets), yes rate on that set's 4th-and-later presentations minus its first 3, averaged over participant-sets having both; observed below the null means people grow more conservative with a concept the more they see the same set (concept tightening/consolidation) beyond what the stationary model and target mix produce, above means they grow more liberal.
results.code:
# name: repeat_exposure_decline
# description: Within each participant x set (participants start where trial_index resets), yes rate on that set's 4th-and-later presentations minus its first 3, averaged over participant-sets having both; observed below the null means people grow more conservative with a concept the more they see the same set (concept tightening/consolidation) beyond what the stationary model and target mix produce, above means they grow more liberal.
def test_statistic(df):
    ti = df["trial_index"].to_numpy()
    pid = np.concatenate([[0], np.cumsum(ti[1:] <= ti[:-1])])
    d = pd.DataFrame({"pid": pid, "s": df["number_set"].to_numpy(),
                      "r": df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)})
    d["rep"] = d.groupby(["pid", "s"]).cumcount()
    d["late"] = d["rep"] >= 3
    m = d.groupby(["pid", "s", "late"])["r"].mean().unstack()
    if True not in m.columns or False not in m.columns:
        return 0.0
    diff = (m[True] - m[False]).dropna()
    return float(diff.mean()) if len(diff) else 0.0

results.name: round_number_target_bias
results.description: Among sets not consisting only of multiples of 10, yes rate to non-example targets that are multiples of 10 minus yes rate to other even non-example targets; observed above the null means people over-endorse salient round numbers beyond what the model's concepts predict, below means the model over-endorses them.
results.code:
# name: round_number_target_bias
# description: Among sets not consisting only of multiples of 10, yes rate to non-example targets that are multiples of 10 minus yes rate to other even non-example targets; observed above the null means people over-endorse salient round numbers beyond what the model's concepts predict, below means the model over-endorses them.
def test_statistic(df):
    parts = df["number_set"].str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric)
    all10 = ((parts % 10 == 0) | parts.isna()).all(axis=1).to_numpy()
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    is_ex = parts.eq(pd.Series(t, index=df.index), axis=0).any(axis=1).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    base = ~all10 & ~is_ex
    a = base & (t % 10 == 0)
    b = base & (t % 2 == 0) & (t % 10 != 0)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: above_minus_below_range
results.description: For targets outside the examples' [min, max] range by 1-15, yes rate above the max minus yes rate below the min; observed above the null means people extend generalization upward (toward larger numbers) more than the model's symmetric interval hypotheses predict, below means they extend downward more.
results.code:
# name: above_minus_below_range
# description: For targets outside the examples' [min, max] range by 1-15, yes rate above the max minus yes rate below the min; observed above the null means people extend generalization upward (toward larger numbers) more than the model's symmetric interval hypotheses predict, below means they extend downward more.
def test_statistic(df):
    parts = df["number_set"].str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric)
    lo = parts.min(axis=1).to_numpy()
    hi = parts.max(axis=1).to_numpy()
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    up = (t > hi) & (t - hi <= 15)
    dn = (t < lo) & (lo - t <= 15)
    if up.sum() == 0 or dn.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[up].mean() - r[dn].mean())

results.name: set_size_two_minus_four
results.description: Yes rate to non-example targets for 2-example sets minus that for 4-example sets; observed above the null means people tighten generalization with more examples more steeply than the model (or are broader after 2 examples), below means the model's size-principle tightening is too strong.
results.code:
# name: set_size_two_minus_four
# description: Yes rate to non-example targets for 2-example sets minus that for 4-example sets; observed above the null means people tighten generalization with more examples more steeply than the model (or are broader after 2 examples), below means the model's size-principle tightening is too strong.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].str.split(",")
    n = df["number_set"].str.count(",") + 1
    tgt = df["target"].astype(int).astype(str)
    is_ex = np.array([t in e for t, e in zip(tgt, ex)])
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    a = (n.to_numpy() == 2) & ~is_ex
    b = (n.to_numpy() == 4) & ~is_ex
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: set_yes_rate_dispersion
results.description: SD across example sets (with >= 10 non-example trials) of the yes rate to non-example targets; observed above the null means people's generalization breadth differs between sets more than the model produces (model too uniform across sets), below means the model exaggerates set-to-set breadth differences.
results.code:
# name: set_yes_rate_dispersion
# description: SD across example sets (with >= 10 non-example trials) of the yes rate to non-example targets; observed above the null means people's generalization breadth differs between sets more than the model produces (model too uniform across sets), below means the model exaggerates set-to-set breadth differences.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].str.split(",")
    tgt = df["target"].astype(int).astype(str)
    is_ex = pd.Series([t in e for t, e in zip(tgt, ex)], index=df.index)
    d = df[~is_ex]
    g = d.groupby("number_set")["rating"].agg(["mean", "size"])
    g = g[g["size"] >= 10]
    return float(g["mean"].std()) if len(g) > 1 else 0.0

results.name: cell_response_variance
results.description: Mean unbiased Bernoulli variance p(1-p)*n/(n-1) of responses within identical (set, target) cells asked >= 3 times; observed below the null means people agree on specific items more than the model's item-level predictions imply (the model is miscalibrated toward 0.5 on items people find clear-cut), above means people are less consistent than the model.
